The following is the transcript of the interview with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian airing on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan" on Sept. 27, 2026. It was recorded on Sept. 25.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Mr. President, thank you for making the time for us.
PRESIDENT MASOUD PEZESHKIAN: In the name of God, the most gracious and the most merciful, I greet you.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Here in New York, Iran's foreign minister presented a proposal to the United States through mediators that would reopen the Strait of Hormuz after seven days if Tehran's conditions were met. At that point, talks about ending the war would begin, and possibly talks about the nuclear program. When do you expect to get a response from the United States?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: If this message reaches the President of the United States, or the interviewers and those involved in the discussions, naturally the process will begin from the very day they accept it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: What would be the conditions to reopen the Strait of Hormuz?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: We had previously reached an agreement based on the MOU that was signed in Pakistan. I signed it, and the President of the United States signed it, and we were proceeding based on that agreement.
We could have continued it, but unfortunately, because of the lack of coordination, the process was interrupted.
Now, in fact, there is a framework along the same path, with the same objectives that were established. Ultimately, the requests that were included in that memorandum and MOU have now been broken down into stages so that we can proceed according to those stages. If the United States agrees to proceed in that way, everything will return to the way it was before. Because right now, it's the United States that has blocked our way, and naturally, Iran has also blocked the way from its side. These are things that both sides need to open up first; then we can sit down at the negotiating table and discuss other issues at hand.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you and President Trump signed this deal back in June, but it fell apart because of the disagreement on the shipping lanes, and then the military, the IRGC, began firing on ships, taking what they called an unauthorized route. Has all that been ironed out? And will Iran charge money for passing through that strait?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: The issue that we had reached an understanding on should, in principle, have been handled according to that understanding. And we are still committed to this MOU and willing to implement it. Naturally, problems may arise along the way. Any process of conflict resolution needs to proceed through dialogue, with some patience and tolerance. But unfortunately, this understanding did not materialize. The deviation from the agreement could have been resolved through dialogue, but ultimately it turned into the breakdown of the understanding. We could have reached this point by talking and resolving the issues. Waiting for a month would not have been difficult. If they had waited for a month, the path would have been reopened automatically in accordance with that understanding, and the remaining stages of the MOU could have continued. But the urgency that developed in the process created a problem.
MARGARET BRENNAN: If President Trump accepts this proposal, can you guarantee your military will abide by it?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: Obviously, we will abide by whatever we commit to. What caused the disagreement in this process, and what led to the dispute along this path, was the failure to reach an agreement that they were supposed to honor, but they did not. The routes that we had agreed upon were supposed to be determined between Iran and Oman, with their coordination, for passage and transit. Basically, if a ship was going to pass outside of those routes, it was supposed to coordinate with them. They didn't, and unfortunately, it led to a confrontation.
If they operate according to that framework, I think all of us will abide by it.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, President Trump said he was open to meeting with you when you were here. That didn't happen. Would you be willing—if you want direct communication—would you be willing to speak directly with him? To meet with him?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: You see what the issue is…now, the atmosphere of distrust that has developed between Iran and the United States is because we have had several rounds of talks with the United States. We reached an understanding on the JCPOA, and after months of negotiations, the U.S. president tore it up, even though we had reached an agreement. Then, after we took responsibility, we sat down and resumed talks with them. In the middle of the negotiations, they attacked us. The bombing began, and the conflict in Iran intensified. Israel came in, and then the United States joined Israel. They martyred many of our commanders and officials, as well as our scientists. Then, after the war, we sat down and resumed talks with them again. Once again, during the talks, they martyred our Supreme Leader, our commanders, and our scientists. They attacked a school and killed and injured innocent children—around 168 schoolchildren who were innocent—and destroyed infrastructure. And after all of that, we sat down and held talks with them again. In the course of those talks, we once again reached an understanding, and once again they broke it. So we are in a situation where we don't know what language we need to--
MARGARET BRENNAN: So no, you wouldn't meet with him?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: Basically, we need to determine now what exactly we want to reach an understanding on. If we don't abide by what we have written down as necessary, can we really resolve it through dialogue? We wrote it down and signed it. It's clear.
The first thing that needs to happen is that the distrust created by this war has to be overcome. We need to abide by what we have written down. The United States needs to show that it does not intend to overthrow our government or our administration. Put yourself in our position. Imagine someone came and martyred your Supreme Leader. And then, not abide by everything you had agreed upon. What would be your reaction? It's not something that can be resolved that simply.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So the offer that you are making for diplomacy, is it now to begin talks about putting limits on Iran's nuclear program but not fully abandoning that program?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: Of course, we agree. We had already reached an understanding on this in our previous talks.They struck it down, we're not supposed to develop nuclear weapons. Within the framework of the NPT and the other existing frameworks, all of these issues are matters that can be agreed upon. Unfortunately, they are disregarding the rights that international law grants to all countries.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Under international law, including the Non-Proliferation Treaty your country signed, though, inspectors would be allowed in from the UN. Will you allow them in now to settle those concerns?
PRESIDENT PEZESHKIAN: That is absolutely correct. According to those very international laws, when there are nuclear centers under the inspections and auspices of the IAEA within the NPT framework, no country has the legal right to attack those nuclear centers and sites. But America and Israel carried out the act of attacking them. Now the agency itself, rather than its strong condemnation, showed absolutely no reaction. Why is it that centers and sites that were completely under their unprecedented surveillance and inspections regime, perhaps they had the most surveillance on those centers. We had no deviation from that framework. Why did they attack it in the first place?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, the IAEA said they were not being given full access. UN inspectors weren't being allowed in. They said they couldn't guarantee the peaceful nature of your program, and say now you have 440 kilograms of 60 percent enriched uranium. So they want to be able to verify that

articles.title_zh: Trump said he would campaign in midterm battlegrounds. He's starting in deep red states instead
articles.content_orig:
Donald Trump seems to be playing defense with his choice of midterm campaign stops in the coming weeks. He’ll soon travel to states where Republicans are suddenly having to defend Senate seats.
Next month, the 80-year-old president will travel to four states where Republicans are supposed to be safe but are suddenly facing competitive Senate races: Texas, Alaska, Iowa, and Florida.
In Texas, where a Democrat hasn’t won a statewide office in over three decades, James Talarico leads Trump-endorsed Attorney General Ken Paxton, 50 percent to 44 percent, according to a Marist poll released this week.
In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola leads incumbent Dan Sullivan by four and five points, according to two polls released two weeks ago.
Iowa Senate candidate Josh Turek, who has Barack Obama’s coveted endorsement, leads Ashley Hinson by eight points in a Marist poll conducted last week.
In Florida, Trump’s home state, polls have favored the GOP, whose Senate and gubernatorial candidates held double-digit leads in a Stetson University survey this week.
Next week, Trump will make very different kinds of stops in deep-red states that have not been a focus of concerned Republicans’ efforts to maintain their slim majorities in Congress. He will appear in Durant, Oklahoma, next Thursday, the Republican National Committee announced . The next day he will stop in Mobile, Alabama, Politico reported . The Trump 47 Committee, the president’s joint fundraiser with the RNC, is hosting each event.
Each state widely backed Trump in the last three presidential elections, meaning the president is sure to revel in past victories. But the utility of stopping there ahead of the midterms is questionable, given how few—if any—races of importance are competitive. Those stops look more like emotional support rallies than attempts to shore up vulnerable Republican candidates.
Each state’s Senate contest is rated “solid” Republican by the Cook Political Report. So are the gubernatorial races . Of the combined 12 House contests in both states, 10 are considered “solid” Republican, and one “solid” Democrat. The outlier is in Alabama’s second congressional district, which the GOP state legislature redrew to carry out Trump’s redistricting effort. The seat, currently held by a Democrat, is now considered “likely” to turn red.
Beginning Oct. 3, Trump will make stops in other “traditional” battleground states, a source told Politico.
The White House referred questions about the president’s schedule to the RNC, which did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast.
Spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Politico: “While Democrats squabble over the last two cents their party has to spare, the president is barnstorming the country, energizing our base, and supercharging Republican candidates in key races and beyond. We have the resources to spend, and Republicans are full steam ahead to protect and expand our majorities.”
With early voting already underway in some states, and amid a flurry of troubling polls on affordability and the Iran war, Republicans have been forced to spend on races that had once been seen as theirs to win. A leaked memo from the Senate GOP’s campaign arm is urging donors to open their wallets for candidates in Alaska, Iowa, and Ohio, where former Sen. Sherrod Brown leads by four points, according to RealClearPolitics’ polling average
Meanwhile, Republicans have all but conceded two Senate seats they had hoped to win not long ago: Georgia and North Carolina.

articles.content_orig:
Usually when divorce battles end, the exes leave the courtroom to lick their wounds and see what’s left in their bank account.
But for Silvio Scaglia, the end of the wrangling over what belongs to him and what belongs to now-ex wife Julia Haart is far from the end of his legal woes — after a judge demanded he be jailed for actions he took during the divorce proceedings.
Last week, we reported that the Italian businessman and his former wife and business partner had ended their four-year $90 million dollar split , with Haart walking away with Elite, the famed modeling agency they ran together during their brief marriage.
Now, according to court papers obtained by Page Six, New York judge Jeffrey Pearlman has issued a no-bail bench warrant for Scaglia’s arrest, demanding he be immediately jailed for 14 days.
Court documents claim that Scaglia broke a law that says spouses aren’t allowed to move shared assets once a divorce has officially begun by transferring the firm — which represents Kendall Jenner, Adriana Lima and more — without Haart’s permission.
The judge said in the papers Scaglia had “siphon[ed]” the onetime couple’s assets as well. As we previously reported, Pearlman had found that the businessman had bought Bentleys, Porsches and Van Cleef & Arpels jewels with company funds.
And Pearlman still wants Scaglia to face the music for ignoring various court orders during the hearings. (Page Six reported in 2024 that the court ordered him to be jailed for ignoring a court order to pay Haart $300,000).
The businessman appears to be living in his native Italy, and has yet to submit to US authorities for any of the alleged crimes.
Court papers, dated Sept. 22, show that the judge found Scaglia in both civil and criminal contempt, saying he knowingly and willfully violated court orders.
Scaglia, who bought Elite in 2011, appointed fashion designer Haart, who is also the star of Netflix reality show “My Unorthodox Life,” as the CEO of the prestigious agency in March 2019, and they married later that year.
Their split in 2022 sparked a bitter series of lawsuits and countersuits over control of Elite and its affiliated companies.
Now, Haart has been awarded 100% of Elite World Group and their $57 million Tribeca apartment after the court found that Scaglia had already transferred the value of his share of the company “and then some” to himself in the form of cash, sports cars and more. Scaglia’s attorneys have previously denied the allegations.
Scaglia and his representatives didn’t respond to our requests for comment.

CNN, MS NOW, and Politico reporters were allowed back into the White House Thursday after a federal judge ordered President Donald Trump to immediately restore their press access.
The re-entry came after a chaotic morning, during which the three outlets filed an emergency request for a hearing, accusing the Trump Administration of having “repeatedly violated” the court order and refusing several reporters access to the White House grounds. "This morning, journalists from each of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico attempted to enter the White House and were turned away, and Secret Service agents confiscated the hard pass of journalists whose hard passes had not previously been confiscated," the outlets said in the court document.
Judge Timothy Kelly had given the Trump Administration until 12:30 p.m. ET to respond to the outlets' filing.
In a court filing of its own, the White House said it "began the process" of reinstating press badges shortly at 7:25 a.m. ET and laid out a timeline of what followed. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Early Thursday, in a District of Columbia court, Judge Kelly issued a temporary restraining order of 14 days against the ban, saying it “likely violated” the media outlets’ “constitutional due process rights.” He ordered that journalists from the banned media outlets should have their White House access reinstated “until further order of the court or the expiration of this temporary restraining order.”
In a statement to TIME, Ted Boutrous, the lawyer representing the news outlets, said “this is a strong ruling vindicating freedom of the press, due process and the rule of law. We greatly appreciate the court’s swift action.”
The order came in response to a lawsuit filed against the Trump Administration by CNN, MS NOW, and Politico on Monday, in which the outlets argued the ban was a “direct assault” on the First Amendment and violated their Fifth Amendment due process rights.
Outlining his ruling, Kelly said the outlets had “shown a likelihood of success, at least on their Fifth Amendment procedural due process claim.” The Fifth Amendment protects Americans from being “deprived of life, liberty, or property, without due process of law.” Kelly determined that the outlets were “likely to succeed in showing that their hard passes were revoked without constitutionally adequate due process.”
The judge also rejected the Trump Administration's assertion that the media ​ban was motivated by “national security” concerns. “Certainly, that is not what President Trump said when he announced that he was ‘banning’ plaintiffs from the WhiteHouse—instead, he focused on the alleged lack of truthfulness and negativity of plaintiffs’ reporting,” Kelly wrote, referencing Trump’s “fake news” reasoning .
The Justice Department, in a legal filing on Tuesday, said the outlets had “received adequate notice” of the ban (a point contested by Kelly) and insisted “the President’s actions are lawful under the First Amendment.”
Ahead of Thursday’s order, Trump dismissed the legal challenge over the ban and indicated he regretted appointing Judge Kelly in 2017.
Vowing to fight any legal block on his ban, Trump insisted : “Almost without question and, as usual, we’ll go for appeal, because fake news people and publications that only write negatively, and who violate our national security by writing false and defamatory stories with unknown ‘sources,’ shouldn’t be allowed access to the [Oval Office].”
However, in the court filing, Kelly stated that “temporary restraining orders are generally unappealable.”
Instead, during the 14-day period, the court “will set a schedule for expedited briefing on a motion for a preliminary injunction,” allowing Trump and the media outlets to submit further evidence for Kelly to consider.
“Either the preliminary injunction will be issued or denied,” says Eugene Volokh, a law professor at UCLA who specializes in the First Amendment. “The temporary restraining order would then lapse, and whichever side loses can then appeal to the D.C. Circuit.”
Instead of an appeal, Trump could file for emergency relief from the D.C. court, similar to how CNN, MS NOW, and Politico did Thursday, according to experts.
But “emergency relief is usually harder to get than a resolution through appeal,” says Volokh.
Trump has a turbulent history with the media. In 2018, he revoked the White House press credentials of Jim Acosta, who was then a CNN correspondent, after a tense exchange during a news conference.
CNN challenged the decision in court and it was Judge Kelly who ordered the White House to reinstate the reporter’s press pass.
Volokh says that legal precedent in the D.C. Circuit, used in both the ongoing case and that of Acosta, has “already been set” for areas of the White House usually open to the media, including the press briefing room.
“The government can't exclude reporters based on viewpoint, and cannot take away a press pass without due process, without some sort of hearing opportunity to be heard, an explanation of what it is that they supposedly did wrong, what rules they violated,” he says.
In light of this, an appeal from the Trump Administration after a preliminary injunction would likely be rejected in the D.C. Circuit, he argues. However, the President may find a better chance in the Supreme Court.
“Generally speaking, the First Amendment does not secure a right of access to government office buildings,” says Volokh, once again noting the exception of areas usually granted access for press. "The same position could be taken by the Supreme Court, and [it] might say: 'Look, the government can pick and choose whom to allow on its property,'" he says.
There has been an outpouring of solidarity among other media outlets in light of the ban.
CNN, one of five U.S. news outlets in the White House press pool that rotates responsibility for pooled live video coverage, was scheduled to cover Trump's trip to the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Monday. When they were restricted from doing so, other major television networks declined to replace CNN’s pool crew.
In a rare joint statement, ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News, and NBC said : “The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No Administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”
In a further show of support, some media publications—including the New York Times and Washington Post —announced they would hold off on publishing or distributing still photographs taken as part of the White House pool coverage.
On Wednesday, 49 media organizations filed a legal brief voicing their support of CNN, MS NOW, and Politico. “Stripping journalists and news outlets of their rights because of perceived editorial viewpoint violates decades of Supreme Court jurisprudence and is impermissible in any type of forum, including the White House,” the brief argued.

articles.content_orig:
A version of this story appeared in CNN’s What Matters newsletter. To get it in your inbox, sign up for free here .
Election Day is fast approaching, but the Supreme Court is still weighing in on the rules — most recently on Friday when it allowed states to use a Trump administration - backed tool to ferret out noncitizen voting there’s little evidence occurs in a widespread way.
Nobody wants noncitizens voting illegally, but the move by justices less than two months from Election Day raises the real concern that legal citizen voters could find themselves unable to cast ballots.
Supreme Court justices have already been faced with multiple questions about the coming election.
They gutted the Voting Rights Act , supercharging a race to redraw congressional maps this year and into the future.
One state, Missouri , was still wondering Friday which congressional districts its voters would cast ballots in come November because lower courts weighed in after the high court. Never mind that ballots had already been printed and mailed.
An unsigned Friday evening decision from the Supreme Court — which sided with opponents of the proposed districts for the third time in as many weeks — seemed likely to put to rest a whirlwind legal saga that bounced through state and federal courts for much of September. Republican Gov. Mike Kehoe said Friday that Missouri would follow the court’s order.
While the justices in other cases blessed the redrawing of maps for partisan gain, they hit pause, at least for now, on the Trump administration’s plan to upend mail-in voting writ large, tabling that issue for the next election.
Noncitizen voting has been a bugbear for Trump for years. He has alleged there is widespread fraud even in elections he won, although neither of his administrations has been able to find much evidence.
I asked CNN’s Fredreka Schouten, a national political writer, about the database this decision unleashes and what it could mean for people trying to cast ballots.
SCHOUTEN: It’s a federal tool known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements. It’s been around for decades and has long been used to verify the citizenship and immigration status of people seeking government benefits. And some election officials have had agreements in the past to use the tool, for a fee, to check the citizenship status of voters.
But the Trump administration dramatically revamped it, starting last year. It’s now linked to lots of government data as part of the administration’s push to hunt for potential noncitizens on the voting rolls.
SCHOUTEN: The SAVE America Act is different but sort of related in that they are both focused on the question of whether only US citizens are casting ballots.
The SAVE America Act would have dramatically revamped voting rules across the country, requiring voter ID to cast a ballot and mandating that people provide documents, such as a birth certificate of US passport, proving their citizenship when they register to vote. It would also put pressure on states to use the SAVE data system and other data tools like it for purging rolls.
Critics say many legitimate voters don’t have easy access to those documents and argue the proposal would have disenfranchised many Americans.
I should say here that experts note that voting by noncitizens in federal elections, which is already illegal, is exceedingly rare. But this has become an animating issue for the president.
SCHOUTEN: The Trump administration linked the information already in SAVE to other federal data, most notably Social Security Administration records, which cover most Americans.
The administration then encouraged election officials to carry out bulk uploads of their states’ registration rolls and waived any fee to do so. Tens of millions of records were run through the system before a federal judge blocked its use earlier this year.
With Friday’s ruling, the US Supreme Court has allowed SAVE to be used again for reviewing voter rolls.
SCHOUTEN: That’s not entirely clear.
The high court’s opinion emphasized that SAVE can be used for “individualized” checks of a voter’s citizenship in the upcoming election but also noted that federal law prohibits mass purges close to Election Day.
But the administration has argued that the federal ban on mass removals within 90 days of an election doesn’t apply to purges involving noncitizens who were improperly registered in the first place. The Supreme Court will decide that question in a case this coming term — but not before the midterms.
SCHOUTEN: Let’s back up a bit.
In addition to encouraging states to use SAVE to conduct their own reviews of their voting rolls, the Justice Department has been on a campaign to obtain each state’s full, unredacted lists of voters, including personal information about voters, such as full dates or birth and partial Social Security numbers, to do its own check on whether states are complying with federal law.
When those states refused, the DOJ sued. So far, the agency has lost all 25 cases in which a judge has ruled.
But federal agencies have moved forward with efforts to try to find potential noncitizens on voting rolls — including using publicly available voter lists. A recent whistleblower complaint released by several Democrats on Capitol Hill alleged that agents in the Department of Homeland Security, who were tasked with rooting out voter fraud, are being kept in the dark about the sources of some of the data being used in their reviews.
And the dispute the Supreme Court was ruling on Friday was the administration’s ability to offer the SAVE systems to states that want to voluntarily want to use it for their own voter list maintenance.
SCHOUTEN: One overarching worry from critics of the SAVE tool is that it’s not reliable.
Take Texas, for example. State officials there ran all 18 million names of its voters through the SAVE tool last year and announced that their audit had found 2,724 potential noncitizens and directed counties to give voters 30 days to verify their citizenship or be removed from the rolls.
Those numbers began dropping once local election officials began digging — in part, because the system doesn’t appear to properly track naturalized citizens.
Earlier this year, I interviewed a Texas resident who became ensnared by the audit. She was born in Argentina and was a naturalized US citizen, yet state officials tagged her as a suspected noncitizen. She was able to quickly send in a scan of her US passport and remain a voter.
Earlier this month, Texas officials announced that hundreds of potential noncitizens flagged last year were indeed Americans and eligible to vote and called on local officials to reinstate their registrations if they had been removed.
SCHOUTEN: If you are worried about this or any other voting issue, you can always verify your registration status with your local election office. There’s enough time before the general election to fix any problems.
CNN’s Tierney Sneed contributed to this report.

The pitching appears to be in a somewhat decent spot (aside from Kevin Gausman hurting himself on Wednesday), but the offense has gone quiet.

articles.title_zh: Trump declares $1B canceled in ‘pocket rescission’ affront to Congress’ funding power
articles.content_orig:
President using rare power to revoke expenditure with bipartisan approval to aid immigrant services
Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1bn in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s office of management and budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending”.
Most of the cuts are focused on services for immigrants, including non-profits that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic president Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by senator Susan Collins, a Republican in a tough re-election campaign and chair of the Senate appropriations committee.
Collins said in a statement the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions”.
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
“This is theft from the American people, plain and simple,” Patty Murray, the Washington Democratic senator, who is vice-chair of the appropriations committee said in a statement . “These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people – not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families. Every Republican who voted for these bills should be furious, because [Russell] Vought is saying their votes don’t count.”
Typically, Congress can review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year. The government accountability office has called the maneuver , known as a “pocket rescission,” illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s constitutional power of the purse”.
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in 50 years by blocking $4.9bn in congressionally approved foreign aid. The US supreme court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a pocket rescission fits part of a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exact greater control over the US government, eroding the power of Congress.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.

Xiang Yu’s razing of the Qin capital Xianyang, which left libraries full of vital texts in ruin, was echoed centuries later in Warsaw
Warsaw’s wartime destruction was not merely the consequence of battle, but a deliberate campaign by its Nazi German occupiers to erase much of the city. In August 1944, the Warsaw Uprising – a Polish armed revolt by the city’s underground resistance against German occupation – began with the aim of liberating Warsaw. German forces fought to crush it, subjecting the city to sustained bombardment.
When the uprising was finally suppressed after nine weeks, the surviving population was expelled, with tens of thousands of Poles sent to concentration camps. The emptied city was then systematically destroyed. German demolition units moved through Warsaw, wrecking or blowing up buildings that had survived the fighting. Churches, palaces, schools, theatres, libraries and historic monuments were reduced to rubble.
By January 1945, almost 90 per cent of the city’s buildings had been destroyed. The cultural losses were particularly devastating. Libraries containing centuries of Polish manuscripts, books, maps and other collections were deliberately burned, while countless works of art and historical records vanished. Warsaw was left in ruins, its historic centre a smouldering pile of debris.

Trial had been set for Monday over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content
TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100m and enact time limits and other restrictions for teenage users, avoiding a trial with a settlement that was modelled on Instagram-owner Meta’s recent agreement with US states.
Alabama described it as a “first-in-the-nation settlement” with a state in the sweeping litigation over social media’s affect on teen wellbeing.
A trial had been set to begin on Monday in the southern US state over claims by Alabama that TikTok misled parents about tools meant to shield children from harmful content.
TikTok’s settlement with Alabama mirrors safety provisions agreed by Meta, including a two-hour daily time limit for teens, restricted access from midnight to 6am, and suspending notifications during school hours.
It will also strengthen age verification, ban beauty filters for teenagers, and offer young users a non-personalised content feed.
Attorney general Steve Marshall hailed Friday’s settlement as “a great day for Alabama parents”. He said: “Tonight, they can rest easier knowing real protections are in place to shield their children from the dangers of social media addiction.”
Under the settlement, TikTok will send $100m to Alabama and could possibly pay up to $300m in total if 40 other attorneys general sign similar agreements with the company within a specified timeframe.
Alabama’s suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States about alleged harm their apps cause young users.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $18bn to settle a sweeping lawsuit brought by US states accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook to get children addicted.
In addition, the Alabama deal includes a conditional restriction that Meta also agreed to: expanding the night-time shutdown period to 10pm to 7am if other platforms also commit to do the same.
“TikTok’s priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community,” a company spokesperson told AFP.
“This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens,” the spokesperson added.
More than a dozen other states, including California and New York, still havesuits against TikTok.
The company has previously settled cases against it that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.
Meta, by contrast, has taken its chances in court – with bruising results.
In March, a jury in New Mexico ordered the Facebook and Instagram owner to pay $375m after finding it had misled the public about the safety of its platforms for children.
That same month, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google’s YouTube negligent in the case of a 20-year-old woman who said she became hooked on social media as a child, awarding her $6m.
Going to trial would have exposed TikTok to unprecedented public scrutiny of how it handles safety, with company documents and executive testimony potentially aired in open court.
Alabama originally sued TikTok and its Chinese parent company ByteDance in April 2025, alleging the app was engineered to hook young users “just like a sophisticated gambling machine”.
The state later narrowed its case to claims under Alabama’s Deceptive Trade Practices Act, focusing on whether TikTok misrepresented the effectiveness of features such as “Restricted Mode” and “Kids Mode.”
The lawsuit accused TikTok of falsely claiming it limits access to sexual and violent content for young users to have its app rated safe for teens in app stores run by Google, Apple and Microsoft and of misleading users about the Chinese government’s access ‌to US users’ data.
TikTok said it designed its platform with teen safety as a key priority and argued that section 230 of the federal Communications Decency Act shields online platforms from liability for user-generated content.

Tyson Fury rips into Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn after latest reports of cancelling their fight
Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua might be off again.
For most of 2026, the boxing world has been waiting for the highly anticipated superfight between British heavyweight champions Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua, but over the past few months, the planned superfight looked to be in dire straits as negotiations hit a snag, primarily based on the location of the bout. Then, earlier this week, things finally appeared to be sorted, with Netflix announcing the bout for Dec. 11 at the 78,000-seat Principality Stadium in Cardiff, Wales .
Unfortunately, immediately after the announcement, more problems arose in the form of UFC CEO Dana White, who Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, insist on not being part of the event. And per reports, that might be the death knell of this fight.
On Friday, boxing reporters Mike Coppinger and Chris Mannix reported that the Fury-Joshua bout is in danger of falling through due to Joshua and Hearn’s insistence on enforcing their contract, which stipulates that UFC CEO Dana White is not involved in the bout, while Turki Alalshikh, who is bankrolling the fight and is also the co-founder of White’s Zuffa Boxing, insists on having White involved.
Following these reports, Fury took to social media to trash Joshua and Hearn for this setback.
“Breaking news, Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight. They’re saying they’re not going to fight now. They’re little shithouse cowards. It’s mainly to do with Eddie Hearn’s ego. He’s making up a million different things, and threatening they’re not going to fight, we’re not going to fight, we’re not going to fight. You little coward. AJ, pull your finger out you little white-flagged, yellow-bellied coward.
“Now we’re coming home. Now I’m coming home. The Gypsy King is coming back to the United Kingdom to thrash you in front of all my fans in Wales, you absolute little nugget, bodybuilding sausage. And now you’re making a million excuses. Now you’ve got Turki Alalshikh finding alternative real men who will fight at the drop of a hat. So I hope you are happy, you little cowardly bastards. I’ve never seen anything like you. You’re pure shithouses, and this is mainly to do with Eddie Hearn’s ego. What a little prick. He’s cost us the biggest fight in boxing history. Clown.”
Joshua and Hearn have yet to respond to these reports or Fury’s comments.
As of now, the Fury-Joshua fight remains planned for December; however, Alalshikh is reportedly looking at other options should the bout fall through.

articles.title_orig: Supreme Court rejects Republicans’ Missouri redistricting push for third time
articles.title_zh: Supreme Court rejects Republicans’ Missouri redistricting push for third time
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — For the third time, the Supreme Court on Friday shut down efforts by Missouri Republicans to use a new congressional map in the midterm elections that are already underway.
The court blocked an appeals court ruling that sought to revive the 2025 map despite two previous Supreme Court decisions and a ruling by the Missouri Supreme Court that ruled against Republicans on the same issue. There were no dissents.
“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the ruling said.
In doing so, the justices granted an emergency application filed by People Not Politicians, the group challenging the new map.
“We are done with corrupt politicians trying to force their map into effect outside the process outlined in the Missouri constitution,” Richard von Glahn, executive director of People Not Politicians Missouri, said in a statement. “We have said from the beginning, people, not politicians will be the final deciders on this DC power grab.”
The election will proceed using a 2022 map that includes six seats held by Republicans and two held by Democrats. The state has already started sending out ballots to military and overseas voters, and some absentee voting began Tuesday.
The high court cited the fact that Missouri has already begun its voting processes.
“This Court has repeatedly cautioned that ‘lower federal courts should not ‘alter the election rules’’ of a state ‘on the eve of an election,’” the ruling said. “The election is not merely upcoming; it has already started.”
The proposed 2025 map would have eliminated one of the Democratic seats, held by Rep. Emanuel Cleaver.
The Missouri map was part of a nationwide push by Republicans at the urging of President Donald Trump to draw new congressional districts that would favor their candidates. Democrats in other states, including California, responded by drawing new maps, too.
Cleaver told NBC News in a brief phone call Friday that he was “very happy” with the ruling and relieved the issue is settled for November.
“It lasted much too long, but it’s over now,” Cleaver said. “The manufactured chaos, you know, has at long last ended, been brought to a final state, and we can move on.”
Cleaver said his campaign will now work to get the word out to voters ahead of the midterm elections in order to address their confusion after the status of their congressional districts has bounced between courts this year.
The St. Louis-based 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Monday ruled that the Republican-drawn Missouri map could be used, but it never went into effect. The Supreme Court’s ruling Tuesday overturns that decision.
The appeals court had ruled the state had to use the 2025 map in part because the primary election had already taken place using it. But in a conflicting ruling, the Missouri Supreme Court said the 2022 map had to be used, while making it clear that Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins, a Republican, was to blame for the confusion.
The state high court ultimately held Hoskins in contempt for his actions.
In its ruling on Friday, the Supreme Court wrote that Hoskins “was well aware that conducting the August primary election with the 2025 map carried significant risks,” citing a May opinion from the state high court that made clear the new map would not go into effect ahead of the 2026 elections.
Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe, a Republican, said in a post on X on Friday that it was “disappointing” that the Supreme Court’s ruling meant the general election will use a different map than the one used in the primary elections.
“Voters deserved consistency and certainty, and not for the rules to be changed between elections,” Kehoe wrote. “Nevertheless, Missouri will follow the Court’s order.”
The court battle started after opponents of the new map gained enough signatures to trigger a state referendum on whether it should be used. Under state law, whenever a state law is subject to a referendum, it is suspended until after the vote takes place.
But Hoskins delayed a decision on whether the referendum push was legitimate until the eve of the primary. He rejected the proposal and ordered the new map to be used.
The Missouri Supreme Court then quickly ruled that there were no grounds to reject the referendum proposal and that, with the issue being put to voters in November, the map should be put on hold and the 2022 districts used instead.
The litigation seemed to be over until a new lawsuit was filed on Sept. 4 by Rick Brattin, the Republican nominee in the district held by Cleaver, as well as Rep. Bob Onder, R-Mo., and two voters.
That moved the fight into federal court, where Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ruled that the new map should be used. That decision ultimately led to the appeals court ruling and Supreme Court intervention.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.
Kyla Guilfoil is a breaking news reporter on the politics team for NBC News Digital.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi visit wraps up with few achievements announced
articles.content_orig:
At the conclusion of Xi's visit, CBS News chief White House correspondent Nancy Cordes asked U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer if the leaders achieved anything new on artificial intelligence.
"I wouldn't say anything new," Greer said. I mean, we've established this this dialogue, AI dialogue with the Chinese, which really is when I think about it, I think of like the red phone between the Kremlin and the White House during the Cold War. And the AI dialogue at a minimum is an opportunity, if the sides feel like they have something they need to share, whether it's risks or other things, we can do it. Most important thing is having a channel."
Greer said there would be "another meeting on AI in the next month or so" although the agenda has not yet been set.
Though Mr. Trump declined to answer shouted questions from reporters about Taiwan during Xi's visit, U.S. ambassador to China David Perdue insisted there is "no change" in the United States' policy toward Taiwan.
" There's no change, no change in the Taiwan policy here," Perdue told CNBC Friday. "He's fully committed to the One China policy. We're committed to the Taiwan Relations Act, the three communiques, and the six assurances. Nothing has changed there. Of course, China has tried to coerce change in that regard. We're not changing the language. We're not changing our position there."
For the last stop of the Chinese leader's state visit, Xi, his wife and the Trumps toured the National Archives briefly on Friday afternoon.
National Archivist Bradford Wilson showed the leaders and their wives the Declaration of Independence and the U.S. Constitution.
Journalists were too far away to hear their conversation, but Mr. Trump did speak briefly to the press.
Asked about his meeting with Xi, the U.S. president said "everything" was accomplished during their meeting, although he didn't elaborate.
During a tea at the White House, Xi thanked the Trumps for the visit.
Through a translator, Xi said everything on their visit was "done to the highest order of perfection" with "thought in every little detail." Xi also said through a translator that he and Mr. Trump "are like two people who are charting the course for the great ship of China-U.S. relations." Xi said they're adding "new substance" to that strategic relationship.
Xi said the two leaders were likely to see each other later this year at the APEC China summit in Shenzhen, and then again at the G20 summit of leaders in the U.S. The G20 is expected to take place at one of Mr. Trump's properties in Miami. Xi welcomed Mr. Trump for a state visit to Beijing in May.
Mr. Trump said he and Xi would be "speaking a lot," adding, "I think our farmers are going to be very happy. A lot of very positive things happened. But America is very happy about this visit and I'm sure China is very happy also. Great things for both countries. And it's been just very, very productive."
The television pool reporter in the room asked Mr. Trump if he asked China to stop sharing intelligence with Iran, but he ignored the question.
David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, told Fox News on Friday that Mr. Trump told Xi it's "unacceptable" for China to be helping Iran in any way with the war. Perdue acknowledged that China has been involved in some assistance that went to Iran directly or indirectly. He also said China has expressed a commitment to not help Iran.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Chinese entities provided satellite images of a base in Jordan to Iran ahead of deadly Iranian strikes that killed three U.S. soldiers and wounded others.
"This has been a continual conversation over some period of time," Perdue told Fox News' Bill Hemmer. "President Xi responded as you might expect. They talked about the U.S. interests. President Trump did a great job making sure that China knows that this is unacceptable. We've seen some movement over the last month as well, but this isn't the first time President Trump has brought it up with President Xi."
Hemmer asked Perdue if that means that China would stop assisting Iran. Perdue said the U.S. has seen "movement" in that direction.
"That's what the commitment is," Perdue responded. "They assured us yesterday they are not doing that. We know that in the past that there was some intel and some potential parts that went to either directly or indirectly. But President Trump again made it very clear, this is unacceptable to us, to have any interaction with Iran with regards to the support of this war."
During remarks at the White House state dinner, Chinese President Xi Jinping said he and President Trump had "sincere and in-depth exchanges" earlier in the day, and "reached common understanding on many issues."
"This has added new substance to the constructive China-U.S. relationship of strategic stability," Xi said through a translator.
Xi did not specify what the two leaders discussed or whether they struck any new agreements, but trade and AI were widely believed to be agenda items. The U.S. and China agreed earlier this week to extend a truce on tariffs for two months, forestalling another trade war for now, though the two countries have not struck a broader deal. The two sides are also rivals on advanced AI, with Mr. Trump arguing for light regulations in order to outpace China. Other major pressure points include China's relationships with Iran and Russia and the future of Taiwan.
Xi briefly recounted the history of U.S.-China ties. He pointed to President George Washington's purchase of Chinese porcelain , the two countries' cooperation during World War II and President Richard Nixon's moves to normalize relations with the People's Republic of China.
He said the U.S. and China have come to "another historic juncture," and argued the two countries' ambitions "can surely be mutually reinforcing."
"China and the United States must act as responsible major countries, meet the expectations of our peoples, keep pace with the trend of our times and explore a new approach for major countries to get along with each other," he said.
President Trump gave his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, a large bald eagle sculpture at the end of his brief remarks at Thursday's state dinner.
During a speech recognizing U.S.-China ties, President Trump offered Chinese President Xi Jinping and other guests a "special treat" — a peek at the construction site for the White House ballroom.
"In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that," the president said, suggesting guests could take a look after the evening's entertainment wraps up.
Mr. Trump speaks about the ballroom frequently, weighing in on design decisions and casting the massive, controversial project as part of his legacy. He has often argued it will allow the White House to host larger state dinners.
"I can tell you that tonight, if we had it, we would've had way more than a thousand people [at the dinner] with standing room only," he said.
In remarks at Thursday's state dinner, President Trump called for the U.S. and China to "continue to build a relationship that promotes prosperity and security for future generations."
Mr. Trump, who has long touted his warm personal relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping, called Xi and his wife "truly outstanding, amazing people."
"As the leaders of our two nations, President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said. "And we've never gotten along better."
Mr. Trump traced the history of U.S.-China relations back to the European explorers who arrived at the American continent while scouring the Atlantic Ocean for new routes to China. He also pointed to early U.S. commercial ties with China, saying the two countries have exchanged "goods, knowledge, customs and ideas."
During a toast to Xi, he said: "May all of our people know a future of harmony, peace and success."

articles.title_orig: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war?
articles.title_zh: Ethiopia fighting: Are Tigray's TPLF forces and the army heading back to war?
articles.content_orig:
Fighting has erupted in Ethiopia's northern region of Tigray between regional forces and the national army.
Tigray residents, who have been trying to recover from a brutal two-year war that ended in 2022, fear a return to full-scale conflict.
There are reports of panic buying - and now internet and call services have been disrupted.
This means people cannot get access to their money via digital apps in what has become a largely cashless society after ATMs stopped working several months ago.
It follows more than six months of worsening relations between the government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that runs Tigray.
The African Union (AU) brokered a peace deal, known as the Pretoria Agreement, between the two sides, ending the war nearly four years ago - but several issues have remained unresolved that have inflamed tensions.
This year, both sides have been trading blame while troops have mobilised amid pockets of fighting.
This week, major clashes erupted in Tigray and quickly spread into the neighbouring Afar and Amhara regions. The two sides disagree over who started the latest escalation.
The TPLF says it was responding to a federal offensive, including drone strikes, while the government says Tigrayan forces attacked first after seizing control of airports in Tigray.
For much of Tigray's modern political history, it has been governed by the TPLF, which first emerged as an armed movement in the 1970s fighting Ethiopia's military government.
It became a major force in the overthrow of the Marxist regime in 1991 and went on to become the most powerful component of the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front (EPRDF), the coalition that governed the ethnically diverse country for nearly three decades.
At times this proved contentious as some felt the TPLF held too much sway as Tigrayans only make up around 6% of Ethiopia's population.
When Abiy Ahmed became prime minister in 2018, he replaced the EPRDF with the Prosperity Party, significantly watering down the TPLF's influence.
Relations between Addis Ababa and the TPLF rapidly deteriorated until war erupted in 2020 in what was one of the most deadly conflicts this century.
The AU mediator estimated some 600,000 people died during the war, which totally cut off Tigray from the outside world and drove the region to the precipice of famine.
An uneasy truce was agreed in November 2022.
There are four key issues - and two concern the fertile area of western Tigray.
The TPLF lost control of this territory in the early days of the war to Amhara, a region which neighbours Tigray to the west and whose fighters had fought on the side of the Ethiopian army.
Many people in Amhara believe the territory of western Tigray should never have been incorporated into Tigray when regional boundaries were redrawn after the military regime was ousted in 1991.
When its fighters seized control during the recent civil war, hundreds of thousands of ethnic Tigrayan people fled and are now living in homeless camps in Tigray and in the capital, Addis Ababa.
The TPLF wants western Tigray back and for those displaced from the territory to return. The government says the future of the territory needs to be decided by a referendum.
For the government, a major matter of contention has been disarmament. It says the TPLF has only handed over old weaponry to the AU and has been hiding its arms.
The two sides have also been at loggerheads over how Tigray should be governed. Under the terms of the deal, an interim administration was appointed by Abiy.
But attempts by the prime minister to influence affairs caused disputes within the TPLF itself and just before the general election in May, which was not held in Tigray because of the security situation, it restored its pre-war administration, disbanding the one set up by Abiy.
This has meant that civil servants are longer being paid and other services have been seizing up, worsening economic conditions.
A major development has seen the TPLF, once politically isolated inside Ethiopia, gain several key allies.
Earlier in September, it joined six other armed movements in forming what is called the Alliance for Survival, which includes those actively fighting the government like Amhara's Fano militia and the Oromo Liberation Army.
Members of the new alliance have different grievances, but they do share one  objective: they want to remove Abiy's government from power.
So while the TPLF and Fano forces were on opposite sides during the civil war - and still disagree over the fate of western Tigray - they have temporarily put some of their differences aside.
TPLF officials say they do not want to repeat the situation of 2020, when they felt surrounded and isolated.
Yet analysts caution the alliance may become difficult to maintain because its members ultimately have very different interests.
As well as blaming the TPLF for starting the recent fighting, it has criticised the new alliance, portraying it as an attempt to destabilise the country.
It has also accused Eritrea of supporting armed groups inside Ethiopia, something Asmara denies.
During the recent civil war, Eritrea fought alongside Ethiopian troops but the two neighbours, which have long had a volatile relationship, have again fallen out.
Their disagreement centres on the Red Sea and its ports.
Ethiopia, the world's most populous landlocked nation, lost access to them when Eritrea seceded in 1993. Recently Prime Minister Abiy has been pushing for ownership of Eritrea's southern port of Assab - about 60km (37 miles) from the border - and hinted at taking it by force.
Reports indicate that federal forces have been using drones and other military operations against Tigrayan forces.
The government's stated justification is that it is responding to attacks and trying to defend federal positions and territory. However, the circumstances surrounding individual strikes are difficult to independently verify.
Residents in one recently targeted town told the BBC the drones had hit two schools, which local officials said had been used by Ethiopian troops as military bases during the war.
This suggests Addis Ababa may believe they are again being used for a military purpose - by Tigrayan forces.
The attacks have come amid reports that the TPLF has been forcibly recruiting young men to join its ranks.
The main diplomatic effort is being led by the AU, which has called for an immediate cessation of hostilities and a return to direct talks.
It has asked former Nigerian President Olusegun Obasanjo, the AU's special Horn of Africa envoy, to engage the parties urgently.
The UN has made a similar appeal, warning against a wider and more devastating conflict.
The regional organisation Igad has also called for fighting to stop and dialogue to resume.
The difficulty is that trust between Addis Ababa and Tigray is extremely low, while the formation of the new armed alliance has made the situation more complicated.
Yes, there is a significant risk of wider conflict inside Ethiopia.
The fighting has already moved to areas over and along Tigray's borders, while the government is simultaneously dealing with armed conflicts in other regions, particularly Amhara and Oromia.
The new alliance potentially connects several of these conflicts politically and militarily.
There is also a fear that Eritrea could be drawn in again - this time against the government.
The two aggressors in Sudan's civil war are also on opposite sides when it comes to allegiances in Tigray, potentially complicating matters.
The AU has specifically urged all neighbouring countries not to take actions that could further escalate the crisis.

articles.title_orig: White House claims pro-Trump ad it paid Fox to air was ‘public service announcement’
articles.title_zh: White House claims pro-Trump ad it paid Fox to air was ‘public service announcement’
articles.content_orig:
Some Democrats say taxpayer-funded ad could be illegal government propaganda aimed at influencing voters
The White House on Friday defended its decision to use taxpayer funds to buy airtime on Fox News for a White House-produced, pro-Trump ad that some Democrats said could be illegal government propaganda aimed at influencing voters in the upcoming midterm elections.
In a lengthy statement sent to news outlets, the White House press office insisted that versions of the ad, which feature audio of Trump urging voters to help him “defeat communism” and a whirlwind video review of his second term, were simply routine “public service announcements” like those produced by previous administrations.
However, while the Trump administration ad features the president in almost every frame, and includes words of praise for him offered by a prominent supporter during the 2024 campaign, none of the advertising from three prior administrations the White House called similar featured any partisan messaging or showed images of Trump’s predecessors.
By contrast, the 30-second version of the pro-Trump ad broadcast on Fox News this week uses audio of Trump telling supporters in Las Vegas last month: “Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America,” and a rapid-fire montage of images of Trump beneath the onscreen text: “America will never be a communist country,” as a chorus sings the words “love me”, taken from a song of that name by JMSN. In the original speech, Trump explicitly identified the enemy as “Dumocrat communists in Congress”.
The last 10 seconds of the ad include text at the bottom the screen saying: “Paid for by the US government.”
The ad aired on Fox News this week as Trump hosted the leader of the world’s largest communist nation, China, for a lavish state visit.
In its new statement, the White House insisted that versions of the ad celebrating Trump, which were also posted on official government accounts on TikTok and YouTube before airing on Fox, “are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action. Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending – at home, at the border, and abroad.”
In fact, the version of the ad broadcast on Fox clearly includes partisan messaging that celebrates Trump’s presidency and features his rhetoric comparing Democrats to communists in the run-up to congressional elections in which he recently urged supporters to “pretend I’m on the ballot” and vote for his party.
Unlike the initial versions of the ad posted on social media, the broadcast version includes onscreen text boasting about what Trump calls his accomplishments. “Largest tax cuts in history,” one slogan reads. “Reigniting American manufacturing,” says another. “Defend law and order and police,” comes next.
The broadcast version of the ad also closes with a tribute to Trump from Dana White, the Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive, who can be heard saying: “He is the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life.” White used that formulation to describe Trump multiple times during the 2024 presidential election campaign, most notably to sing Trump’s praises at the Republican national convention .
While the White House argues that the ad is an “unapologetically American” public service announcement “aimed at the country – not a line on the ballot”, the actual images used are not of the grandeur of the country or its people, but just its current president.
In fact, slowing down the rapid-fire montage reveals that the flash-frame imagery in the ad is exclusively of Trump commanding the stage in a bizarre mix of moments during his second term, including: overseeing the US military raid on Venezuela; hosting a state dinner for Saudi crown prince Mohammed bin Salman; accepting the Fifa peace prize; pardoning a turkey; announcing a new class of US navy ships to be named for himself; attending a Kennedy Center performance; awarding the Fifa Club World Cup trophy; showing Cristiano Ronaldo his presidential walk of fame; and addressing McDonald’s owners.
The paid advertising by prior administrations which the Trump White House compared its ad to on Friday were uniformly non-partisan public information campaigns. A 2002 Super Bowl ad from the White House office of national drug control policy, which connected drug use by young Americans to funding terrorist attacks, made no mention of political parties or then president George W Bush. A 2015 ad showing people how much money they could save by signing up for health insurance at healthcare.gov did not show or mention Barack Obama. A 2021 ad from the department of health and human services to promote the Covid-19 vaccine similarly made no mention of the president at the time, Joe Biden.
The White House defense of its ad comes after the representative Jamie Raskin, a Maryland Democrat and constitutional scholar, suggested on social media that the ad may violate federal laws including the Hatch Act.
“This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes,” Raskin wrote . “It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it. It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns.”
AdImpact, a firm that tracks political ads, told the Wall Street Journal that the pro-Trump ad aired on Fox News in New York City, Los Angeles, Miami and Washington DC, as well as on Newsmax in Chicago.
The administration has spent at least $443,000 so far to air that ad, according to the Associated Press.
AdImpact reported on Friday that the White House also paid to broadcast a second ad featuring Trump, with excerpts from his 3 July address at Mount Rushmore. The second ad, which aired on the rightwing network Newsmax on Friday, includes images of the president’s supporters waving Trump flags and ends with the president repeating a slogan he has used dozens of times to describe his second administration: “This is only the beginning of the golden age of America.”
JMSN, the Detroit-born artist who wrote and performs the song Love Me, wrote on social media that it had been used “illegally”, because he was not approached by the White House for permission. “I would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign,” the singer wrote. “I am looking at lawyers handling this.”

articles.title_zh: Supreme Court lets Trump administration use revamped federal voter eligibility database for now
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court on Friday permitted the Trump administration to use an expanded federal database containing citizenship information, as the president encourages states to purge people from voter rolls.
The justices, divided 6-3 on ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, granted an emergency request filed by the government after lower courts ruled that the Trump administration’s changes to the database were likely unlawful.
Critics have said the data is unreliable and could lead to U.S. citizens being kicked off the voter rolls.
But the court noted in its unsigned ruling that the National Voter Registration Act bars the broad purging of voter rolls in the weeks leading up to an election, which “limits the potential impact” of the decision this year. States can still make individualized queries about voters.
On the broader legal questions raised in the case, the court said that federal law requires the government to respond to requests from states for information about citizenship.
The lower court injunction “prevents the federal government from using the program it believes is best suited to the task,” the court said.
In dissent, liberal Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote that the government had not done enough to show that the lower court ruling needed to be blocked.
In her view, “the harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the nonexistent harm that the Government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take,” she added.
Various groups challenging the plan, led by the League of Women Voters, have argued that it violates several laws, including the Social Security Act and the Privacy Act.
The Supreme Court decision “puts millions of Americans at risk for being unlawfully targeted by the administration’s unreliable voter purge database,” the groups said in a statement.
Conservative who have backed the administration’s efforts to tighten voting laws, welcomed the decision.
The ruling “just makes it easier for states to get federal citizenship data to help them clean up voter rolls,” Jason Snead, executive director of the Honest Elections Project, said in a statement.
The Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements program, known as SAVE, was set up by Congress in 1986 so that government agencies could quickly determine someone’s immigration status when they applied for benefits like Social Security.
The Trump administration expanded SAVE after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March 2025 that required agencies to take steps to better ensure that only U.S. citizens vote in elections.
The government expanded the database by adding information from the Social Security Administration, which enabled searches using Social Security numbers and allowed officials to do bulk searches.
After states started putting their voter rolls through the newly expanded system, some local officials noticed mistakes; many of the flagged registrants were newly naturalized citizens, according to reporting from ProPublica and The Texas Tribune .
Texas was one of the first states to put its full voter rolls — more than 18 million registrations — through the SAVE database last year. Just three people have been charged with voting illegally as a noncitizen.
A federal judge blocked the Trump administration plan, with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit reaching the same conclusion.
In court papers, Solicitor General D. John Sauer said that the district court’s ruling “threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by preventing the government from responding to state requests to verify the citizenship of potential voters.
Opponents argue the expanded database could force bureaucratic obligations on newly naturalized citizens who are asked to prove their citizenship after being flagged by the system.
Noncitizen voting is extremely rare. All states are required to conduct voter roll list maintenance under federal law, and states already have processes to identify any noncitizens who do accidentally make it onto the voter rolls.
Lawrence Hurley is a senior Supreme Court reporter for NBC News.
